rationale: While global developmental delay and severe-to-profound intellectual disability (HP:0001263) are virtually universal (present in nearly 100% of assessed patients over 3 years of age across cohorts), intractable early-onset seizures (HP:0001250) do not meet the hypothesized >90-95% threshold across all documented individuals. In the largest comprehensive systematic cohort (Leitão et al., 2026; n = 141), epilepsy is reported in approximately 85% of patients, with at least 16 documented affected individuals lacking seizures entirely. Furthermore, median seizure onset in some cohorts is 24 months rather than neonatal/early infantile onset, contradicting the claim that early-onset refractory seizures are present in virtually all individuals.

evidence.text: In a systematic analysis of 141 individuals with RNU2-2 variants (35 dominant, 91 recessive across 73 families), all individuals older than 3 years had intellectual disability except one, but 16 individuals were explicitly identified without epilepsy (approx. 85% penetrance of epilepsy overall).

source.quote: Patients with RNU2-2 DEE had median seizure onset age of 24 months, focal and generalized seizures, status epilepticus (n = 5), severe to profound impairment, hyperventilation (n = 3), and obstructive sleep apnea (n = 3).

evidence.text: Biallelic variants in RNU2-2 manifest as a severe developmental and epileptic encephalopathy and represent a highly frequent unrecognized cause of neurodevelopmental disorder with seizures.

source.title: Biallelic variants in RNU2-2 cause a remarkably frequent developmental and epileptic encephalopathy
source.quote: We define a recessive RNU2-2 syndrome, delineate its unique genetic architecture and show that it manifests clinically as a severe developmental and epileptic encephalopathy.

conflicts: Epilepsy penetrance: While global developmental delay/ID is observed in >95% of individuals older than 3 years, Leitão et al. report 16 of 141 individuals lacking epilepsy (~85% penetrance), directly refuting the hypothesis that seizures are present in >90-95% of all RNU2-2-associated disease cases.

Age of seizure onset: The hypothesis posits early-onset seizures, but Chiu et al. reported a median seizure onset age of 24 months, indicating childhood rather than early infantile onset in substantial portions of the cohort.

new_directions.question_text: Does epilepsy penetrance and age of onset differ significantly between dominant de novo RNU2-2 variants and recessive biallelic RNU2-2 variants?
new_directions.rationale: Leitão et al. and Jackson et al. describe both dominant and recessive RNU2-2-associated disorders, but dominant versus recessive sub-cohort seizure rates and phenotypes need stratification to evaluate whether DEE119 strict definition accounts for non-epileptic neurodevelopmental phenotypes.

new_directions.question_text: What is the discriminatory diagnostic power of combining hyperkinesia/movement disorders and sleep apnea/hyperventilation with intellectual disability to distinguish RNU2-2 DEE from other noncoding spliceosomopathies such as RNU4-2?
new_directions.rationale: Both Henry et al. and Chiu et al. note distinctive features (hyperkinesia, hyperventilation, sleep apnea, hippocampal sclerosis) which could allow clinicians to phenotype RNU2-2 patients apart from RNU4-2 ReNU syndrome.
